analysis.title: Democrats ride a blue wave
key_insights: Democrats won both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterms. This was the consensus base case, but the margins were larger than almost anyone expected.
In the House, Democrats clinched control with 68 seats still pending, a net gain of 25 seats against the 3 needed for a majority. The final gain is likely to be larger than 25.
In the Senate, Democrats have a net gain of 7 seats against the 4 needed for control. Two seats are still uncalled, and a final gain of 8 or 9 is possible.
Mississippi, which Trump won by about 23 points in 2024, is one of the two uncalled Senate races. CA-CIB calls this the most astonishing result and a sign of how comprehensive the defeat was.
Alaska's Senate result may take a while to finalize. It uses ranked choice voting, and mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day are accepted until 18 November.

CA-CIB still expects legislative gridlock, meaning no major new legislation, especially on fiscal matters such as spending packages or tax changes. Even a net gain of 9 Senate seats falls short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster, and a Trump veto would still apply.

A government shutdown could go either way. One-party control of Congress could ease a funding deal, but Trump might veto bills so that Democrats take the blame. Funding next expires on 11 December, before the new Congress takes office.

Trump's first reaction was conciliatory, with a pledge to accept the results and talk of working with Democrats. CA-CIB notes he has a history of being mercurial and could revert to his pledge to veto everything, asserting himself where he can act without Congress, such as trade and foreign policy.
Some Republicans may become more willing to cross Trump, since his policy choices and weak candidate picks likely contributed to the defeat. His grip on party dissent may loosen.
Democrats also gained governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. Texas was a surprise, because Senate candidate Ken Paxton had been seen as more vulnerable than Governor Greg Abbott.

CA-CIB does not expect major AI regulation from Washington because of the likely Trump veto. New Democratic governors who are more hostile to data centre construction could delay or relocate projects, but CA-CIB does not expect them to derail the AI buildout.

CA-CIB does not think the midterm momentum carries over to 2028. It reads the result as a repudiation of Trump more than an endorsement of Democrats, whose party favourability is still below 40% per RealClearPolitics.

Betting markets and many observers had seen JD Vance as the strong favourite for the 2028 Republican nomination. CA-CIB sees a rising chance that Republicans distance themselves from Trump instead of defaulting to his vice president.
risk_factors: Trump could veto legislation from a Democratic Congress, or assert himself through trade and foreign policy, where he can act without Congress.
A government shutdown risk remains, with funding next expiring on 11 December.
Local opposition from Democratic governors could delay or relocate data centre projects.
Democrats could squander momentum if they push aggressively for the preferences of the left wing of the party.

tension_points.bull_case: One party controlling both chambers of Congress could make it easier to reach a funding agreement the first time the issue comes up in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: Trump could veto funding legislation from a Democratic Congress, expecting Democrats to take the blame for a shutdown if they control both chambers.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Trump veto of funding legislation from the Democratic Congress would invalidate the case for an easier agreement.

theme_stances.key_argument: Democrats would still fall short of a filibuster-proof 60 seats, and a Trump veto would still apply.
theme_stances.evidence: we are not convinced it really changes much
